analysis.one_liner: Sets patient protections for managed care plans: appeals of claim denials, access to specialists and emergency care, and the right to sue.
analysis.headline: The Bipartisan Patient Protection Act of 2004, a revived version of the patients' rights fight, was referred to the Senate health committee and never received a hearing, a vote, or a floor action before the 108th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would force health plans to give patients a real process to contest denied care: a quick decision on requests for treatment, an internal appeal by someone not involved in the first denial, and an outside review by independent doctors whose decision binds the plan. It would guarantee direct access to obstetricians, pediatricians, and specialists; cover emergency care and minimum hospital stays after mastectomies; pay for patients in clinical trials; ban insurers from penalizing doctors for fighting for patients; and for the first time let people in employer plans sue when a denial hurts them. It was referred to the Senate HELP committee in February 2004 and died there with no further action, no hearing, no vote, and no cosponsors.
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly 160 million Americans covered by employer-based or private health insurance, and especially people denied coverage for a test, drug, specialist visit, or hospital stay who currently have little practical recourse under a 1974 federal law that blocks them from suing. Also doctors whose medical judgment is overridden by plan reviewers, and women seeking direct OB-GYN access and mastectomy stays.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People in private and employer health plans

how_it_helps.text: Requires plans to decide requests for treatment quickly — within 72 hours when a doctor certifies delay would jeopardize life or health — and to tell patients why in plain language when care is denied [S3].

Gives patients an internal appeal reviewed by someone who took no part in the original denial, and then an independent external review by doctors with no financial ties to the plan, whose decision is binding on the plan, with penalties up to $10,000 per violation for plans that refuse to comply [S3].
Guarantees direct access to OB-GYN and pediatric care, timely access to specialists, coverage of emergency care, continued care with a treating doctor, and access to needed prescription drugs [S3].

Requires coverage of a minimum hospital stay after a mastectomy or lymph node dissection for breast cancer and access to a second consultation, and lets patients in federally approved clinical trials keep their coverage [S3].
Bars plans from using compensation schemes that reward employees or contractors for denying claims, and prohibits interference with doctor-patient communications and with patient advocacy [S3].

Amends the Employee Retirement Income Security Act so patients in employer plans can obtain civil remedies — including the right to sue for damages — and requires courts to treat the loss of a nonwage-earning spouse or parent as an economic loss to be fully compensated, closing a loophole that had capped recoveries at the value of denied medical bills [S3, S2].
Funds state health care consumer assistance offices to help people navigate denials and appeals [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers and employer-sponsored health plans, which would bear the cost of faster decisions, independent reviews they must pay for and comply with, expanded guaranteed coverage, and new legal liability when their denial of care injures a patient. Some of that cost could be passed back to consumers as premiums.
analysis.who_pays_short: Health insurers and employer health plans

drawbacks.text: The outside appeals process is layered: plans can require a filing fee up to $25, a written request, exhaustion of internal review, and can screen out denials that turn on plan exclusions or cost-sharing rather than medical judgment, so some patients would still be left without a meaningful review [S3].
Insurers warned that mandates and new liability would raise premiums and that some employers would drop coverage, a cost concern that shaped the broader patients' rights debate [S2].

The bill reached 11 words in committee in February 2004 with zero cosponsors — not even from the Republicans its 'bipartisan' title invoked — so its actual provisions never faced amendment or public hearing, and any claim about their final effect is untested [S4, S5].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For patients facing a denial, the right to a fast decision, an independent reviewer, and the ability to sue weighs heavily against insurers' administrative costs. The main design risk is that plans could still bury patients in process — internal appeals, filing fees, screening of non-medical denials — and that premiums could rise; a fair version of that debate never happened because the bill never got a hearing.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate referred the bill to its Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee on the day it was introduced in February 2004, and no hearing, markup, vote, or floor action ever followed before the 108th Congress ended in January 2005.

narrative.text: Senator Barbara Boxer introduced the bill on February 12, 2004 and spoke for it on the Senate floor the same day [S5].
The Senate referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions on the day of introduction [S5].
No further action — no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote — appears in the full action history for the remainder of the 108th Congress, which ended January 3, 2005 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers and self-insured employers are better off: the bill that would have subjected their coverage denials to binding independent review and new lawsuits died in committee without ever being debated. Patients denied care in 2004-2005 remained governed by the pre-existing rules that gave them no right to sue.

for.name: Sen. Barbara Boxer
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the Senate floor on February 12, 2004.

against.name: Senate HELP Committee
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on February 12, 2004 and took no action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Senate Majority Leader
against.role: Controlled the Senate floor calendar in the 108th Congress
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the floor; as its party held the majority and the committee, the bill died without floor consideration.

sides.party_line_note: With one sponsor, no cosponsors, and no votes, the record shows no partisan pattern — only that the bill never advanced past referral.

industries.industry: Health insurers and managed care plans
industries.note: The bill would end their ability to quietly deny care, require them to pay for independent reviewers whose decisions bind them, and expose them to lawsuits for harmful denials. The bill dying preserves the status quo in which denial decisions face little outside check.
ERISA plans would face the same standards and, for the first time, civil remedies for patients, which employers have long resisted. The bill's death leaves their liability shield intact.

industries.industry: Utilization review and external review contractors
industries.note: The bill mandates certified independent review entities and requires plans to bear review costs, creating paid work for these contractors. Their gain comes from enforcing patient rights rather than restricting them.
Guaranteed direct access, specialist referral timelines, and protection against plan interference with doctor-patient communication strengthen physicians' role versus insurers.
